current_example.title: Example: Solving an Equation Governing the Current in an RCL Circuit: Sinusoidal EMF

q-345269.name: Question 1
q-345269.problem:
A series RCL circuit has a source electromotive force (EMF) of $9\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\,\text{V},$ a resistance of $18\,Ω,$ a capacitance of $0.002\,\text{F},$ and an inductance of $L=9\,\text{H}.$ Find the differential equation governing the amount of current $I$ (in amperes) in the circuit at time $t$ (in seconds).

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*
q-345269.worked_solution:
The diagram for our circuit is shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14186466/assets/a3bbe131778b11fe61a7e436d3d4729958bb207961ca9faaac91250cf4f2dde0.png)

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=18\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=18I.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{0.002}=500q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=9\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=9\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$
9\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)=18I+500q+9\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(9\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) & =\frac{d}{dt}(18I+500q+9\,\frac{dI}{dt}) \\ 27\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) & =18\,\frac{dI}{dt}+500\,\frac{dq}{dt}+9\,\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}+\frac{500}{9}I=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t).
$$

q-345269.html:
Question 1
?

A series RCL circuit has a source electromotive force (EMF) of 9sin⁡(3t)V, a resistance of 18Ω, a capacitance of 0.002F, and an inductance of L=9H. Find the differential equation governing the amount of current I (in amperes) in the circuit at time t (in seconds).

Hint: The voltage drop VC across the capacitor is related to its charge by q=CVC, where C is the capacitance measured in Farads.

a
d2Idt2+18dIdt+500I=27cos⁡(3t)
b
d2Idt2+4dIdt+5009I=3cos⁡(3t)
c
d2Idt2+2dIdt+5009I=3sin⁡(3t)
d
d2Idt2+2dIdt+5009I=27cos⁡(3t)
e
d2Idt2+2dIdt+5009I=3cos⁡(3t)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The diagram for our circuit is shown below.

The current I, measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge q, measured in coulombs. I=dqdt

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

  • The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality R=18Ω. So, VR=18I.

  • The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by q=CVC. Therefore, VC=qC=q0.002=500q.

  • The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality L=9H. Hence, VL=9dIdt.

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

9sin⁡(3t)=18I+500q+9dIdt.

Differentiating with respect to t, the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

ddt(9sin⁡(3t))=ddt(18I+500q+9dIdt)27cos⁡(3t)=18dIdt+500dqdt+9d2Idt2,

which, when substituting in I=dqdt, gives

d2Idt2+2dIdt+5009I=3cos⁡(3t).

q-345057.name: Question 2
q-345057.problem:
A series RCL circuit has a source electromotive force (EMF) of $10\,\text{V},$ a resistance of $32\,Ω,$ a capacitance of $0.005\,\text{F},$ and an inductance of $L=8\,\text{H}.$ Find the differential equation governing the amount of current $I$ (in amperes) in the circuit at time $t$ (in seconds).

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*
q-345057.worked_solution:
The diagram for our circuit is shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14186466/assets/ddb44fa46fed9427723f2ff5f6fd31011271f411d5dbc58e232bc5b8bbd86607.png)

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=32\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=32I.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{0.005}=200q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=8\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=8\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$
10=32I+200q+8\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(10) & =\frac{d}{dt}(32I+200q+8\,\frac{dI}{dt}) \\ 0 & =32\,\frac{dI}{dt}+200\,\frac{dq}{dt}+8\,\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+4\,\frac{dI}{dt}+25I=0.
$$

q-345057.html:
Question 2
?

A series RCL circuit has a source electromotive force (EMF) of 10V, a resistance of 32Ω, a capacitance of 0.005F, and an inductance of L=8H. Find the differential equation governing the amount of current I (in amperes) in the circuit at time t (in seconds).

Hint: The voltage drop VC across the capacitor is related to its charge by q=CVC, where C is the capacitance measured in Farads.

a
d2Idt2+2dIdt+25I=54
b
d2Idt2+2dIdt+25I=0
c
d2Idt2+4dIdt+25I=0
d
d2Idt2+4dIdt+100I=0
e
d2Idt2+4dIdt+25I=54
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The diagram for our circuit is shown below.

The current I, measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge q, measured in coulombs. I=dqdt

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

  • The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality R=32Ω. So, VR=32I.

  • The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by q=CVC. Therefore, VC=qC=q0.005=200q.

  • The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality L=8H. Hence, VL=8dIdt.

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

10=32I+200q+8dIdt.

Differentiating with respect to t, the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

ddt(10)=ddt(32I+200q+8dIdt)0=32dIdt+200dqdt+8d2Idt2,

which, when substituting in I=dqdt, gives

d2Idt2+4dIdt+25I=0.

q-345149.name: Question 3
q-345149.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14186466/assets/4852aaf3945331346a68fe3f967658665f71d81be0e28fd0d34fd965c7045596.png)

Find the differential equation governing the current $I$ (in amperes) at time $t$ (in seconds) in the circuit given in the diagram above.

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*
q-345149.worked_solution:
The diagram shows a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $6\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $10\,Ω,$ a capacitor of capacitance $0.005\,\text{F},$ and an inductor of inductance $2\,\text{H}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=10\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=10I.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{0.005}=200q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=2\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=2\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$
6\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)=10I+200q+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(6\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)) & =\frac{d}{dt}(10I+200q+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}) \\ 24\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) & =10\,\frac{dI}{dt}+200\,\frac{dq}{dt}+2\,\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+5\,\frac{dI}{dt}+100I=12\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t).
$$

q-345149.html:
Question 3
?

Find the differential equation governing the current I (in amperes) at time t (in seconds) in the circuit given in the diagram above.

Hint: The voltage drop VC across the capacitor is related to its charge by q=CVC, where C is the capacitance measured in Farads.

a
d2Idt2+5dIdt+100I=12cos⁡(4t)
b
d2Idt2+10dIdt+200I=24cos⁡(4t)
c
d2Idt2+5dIdt+100I=12sin⁡(4t)
d
2d2Idt2+10dIdt+200I=24cos⁡(4t)
e
d2Idt2+5dIdt+100=12cos⁡(4t)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The diagram shows a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of 6sin⁡(4t)V, a resistor of resistance 10Ω, a capacitor of capacitance 0.005F, and an inductor of inductance 2H.

The current I, measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge q, measured in coulombs. I=dqdt

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

  • The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality R=10Ω. So, VR=10I.

  • The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by q=CVC. Therefore, VC=qC=q0.005=200q.

  • The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality L=2H. Hence, VL=2dIdt.

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

6sin⁡(4t)=10I+200q+2dIdt.

Differentiating with respect to t, the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

ddt(6sin⁡(4t))=ddt(10I+200q+2dIdt)24cos⁡(4t)=10dIdt+200dqdt+2d2Idt2,

which, when substituting in I=dqdt, gives

d2Idt2+5dIdt+100I=12cos⁡(4t).
q-345149.knowledge_point: Constructing an Equation Governing the Charge in an RCL Circuit

q-343955.name: Question 4
q-343955.problem:
A series RCL circuit has a source electromotive force (EMF) of $12\,\text{V},$ a resistance of $40\,Ω,$ a capacitance of $0.005\,\text{F},$ and an inductance of $L=20\,\text{H}.$ Find the differential equation governing the amount of current $I$ (in amperes) in the circuit at time $t$ (in seconds).

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*
q-343955.worked_solution:
The diagram for our circuit is shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14186466/assets/169844e6d45393119ac1579cc89e34850401810bfcc1c7537d5b72851a0b2b02.png)

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=40\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=40I.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{0.005}=200q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=20\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=20\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$
12=40I+200q+20\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(12) & =\frac{d}{dt}(40I+200q+20\,\frac{dI}{dt}) \\ 0 & =40\,\frac{dI}{dt}+200\,\frac{dq}{dt}+20\,\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}+10I=0.
$$

q-343955.html:
Question 4
?

A series RCL circuit has a source electromotive force (EMF) of 12V, a resistance of 40Ω, a capacitance of 0.005F, and an inductance of L=20H. Find the differential equation governing the amount of current I (in amperes) in the circuit at time t (in seconds).

Hint: The voltage drop VC across the capacitor is related to its charge by q=CVC, where C is the capacitance measured in Farads.

a
d2Idt2+2dIdt+10I=35
b
d2Idt2+10dIdt+50I=3
c
d2Idt2+4dIdt+10I=0
d
d2Idt2+2dIdt+10I=0
e
d2Idt2+4dIdt+10I=35
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The diagram for our circuit is shown below.

The current I, measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge q, measured in coulombs. I=dqdt

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

  • The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality R=40Ω. So, VR=40I.

  • The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by q=CVC. Therefore, VC=qC=q0.005=200q.

  • The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality L=20H. Hence, VL=20dIdt.

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

12=40I+200q+20dIdt.

Differentiating with respect to t, the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

ddt(12)=ddt(40I+200q+20dIdt)0=40dIdt+200dqdt+20d2Idt2,

which, when substituting in I=dqdt, gives

d2Idt2+2dIdt+10I=0.

q-345414.name: Question 5
q-345414.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14186466/assets/dfe6902183d348f21d053acce448bd5012d190b6b678f406099ef9d0a2c83374.png)

Find the differential equation governing the current $I$ (in amperes) at time $t$ (in seconds) in the circuit given in the diagram above.

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*
q-345414.worked_solution:
The diagram shows a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $7\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $10\,Ω,$ a capacitor of capacitance $0.02\,\text{F},$ and an inductor of inductance $2\,\text{H}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=10\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=10I.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{0.02}=50q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=2\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=2\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$
7\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)=10I+50q+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(7\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)) & =\frac{d}{dt}(10I+50q+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}) \\ -21\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & =10\,\frac{dI}{dt}+50\,\frac{dq}{dt}+2\,\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+5\,\frac{dI}{dt}+25I=-10.5\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

q-345414.html:
Question 5
?

Find the differential equation governing the current I (in amperes) at time t (in seconds) in the circuit given in the diagram above.

Hint: The voltage drop VC across the capacitor is related to its charge by q=CVC, where C is the capacitance measured in Farads.

a
d2Idt2+5dIdt+25I=10.5sin⁡(3t)
b
d2Idt2+5dIdt+50I=−10.5sin⁡(3t)
c
d2Idt2+5dIdt+25I=−10.5cos⁡(3t)
d
d2Idt2+5dIdt+25I=−10.5sin⁡(3t)
e
d2Idt2+10dIdt+25I=−21sin⁡(3t)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The diagram shows a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of 7cos⁡(3t)V, a resistor of resistance 10Ω, a capacitor of capacitance 0.02F, and an inductor of inductance 2H.

The current I, measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge q, measured in coulombs. I=dqdt

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

  • The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality R=10Ω. So, VR=10I.

  • The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by q=CVC. Therefore, VC=qC=q0.02=50q.

  • The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality L=2H. Hence, VL=2dIdt.

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation 7cos⁡(3t)=10I+50q+2dIdt.

Differentiating with respect to t, the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is ddt(7cos⁡(3t))=ddt(10I+50q+2dIdt)−21sin⁡(3t)=10dIdt+50dqdt+2d2Idt2,

which, when substituting in I=dqdt, gives d2Idt2+5dIdt+25I=−10.5sin⁡(3t).

q-345169.name: Question 6
q-345169.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14186466/assets/d34d844ed99307f03ff2454f8916efa91738d7b967f546ef6e516e003d4fc481.png)

Find an equation for the current (in amperes) in the circuit given in the diagram above, expressing your answer in terms of time $t$ (in seconds) only, and given that the initial charge on the capacitor is $\frac{1}{4}\,\text{C}$ and the initial current is $1\,\text{A}.$

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*
q-345169.worked_solution:
The diagram shows a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $9\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $12\,Ω,$ a capacitor of capacitance $0.0625\,\text{F},$ and an inductor of inductance $2\,\text{H}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=12\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=12I.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{0.0625}=16q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=2\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=2\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$
9=12I+16q+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(9) & =\frac{d}{dt}(12I+16q+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}) \\ 0 & =12\,\frac{dI}{dt}+16\,\frac{dq}{dt}+2\,\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+6\,\frac{dI}{dt}+8I=0.
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear homogeneous equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must take a linear combination of two linearly independent solutions.

Assuming the solutions take the form $I={e}^{\lambda t},$ we obtain two solutions, namely, $I={e}^{-4t}$ and $I={e}^{-2t}.$
So, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)=A{e}^{-4t}+B{e}^{-2t}.
$$

We're told that the circuit starts with an initial charge of $\frac{1}{4}\,\text{C}$ on the capacitor and an initial current of $1\,\text{A}.$
Now, solving the Kirchhoff's law equation for $\frac{dI}{dt},$ we have

$$
\frac{dI}{dt}=\frac{9}{2}-6I-8q.
$$

So, we can apply the initial conditions $I(0)=1$ and 

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}^{′}(0) & =\frac{9}{2}-6I(0)-8q(0) \\  & =\frac{9}{2}-6\cdot 1-8\cdot \frac{1}{4} \\  & =-\frac{7}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

and solve for $A$ and $B.$

- Substituting $I(0)=1$ into our general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =A{e}^{-4(0)}+B{e}^{-2(0)} \\ 1 & =A+B.\end{aligned}
$$

- Differentiating $I,$ we get

$$
{I}^{′}=-4A{e}^{-4t}-2B{e}^{-2t}
$$

Substituting in ${I}^{′}(0)=-\frac{7}{2}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{7}{2} & =-4A{e}^{-4(0)}-2B{e}^{-2(0)} \\ -\frac{7}{2} & =-4A-2B.\end{aligned}
$$

Putting the two equations in $A$ and $B$ together gives the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}1=A+B \\ -\frac{7}{2}=-4A-2B\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $A=\frac{3}{4}$ and $B=\frac{1}{4}.$ Therefore, the equation for the current (in amperes) in the circuit is

$$
I(t)=\frac{3}{4}{e}^{-4t}+\frac{1}{4}{e}^{-2t}.
$$

q-345169.html:
Question 6
?

Find an equation for the current (in amperes) in the circuit given in the diagram above, expressing your answer in terms of time t (in seconds) only, and given that the initial charge on the capacitor is 14C and the initial current is 1A.

Hint: The voltage drop VC across the capacitor is related to its charge by q=CVC, where C is the capacitance measured in Farads.

a
I(t)=34e−4t+14e−2t
b
I(t)=34e−2t+14e−4t
c
I(t)=14e−4t+34e−2t
d
I(t)=34e−4t−14e−2t
e
I(t)=74e−4t+14e−2t
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The diagram shows a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of 9V, a resistor of resistance 12Ω, a capacitor of capacitance 0.0625F, and an inductor of inductance 2H.

The current I, measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge q, measured in coulombs. I=dqdt

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

  • The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality R=12Ω. So, VR=12I.

  • The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by q=CVC. Therefore, VC=qC=q0.0625=16q.

  • The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality L=2H. Hence, VL=2dIdt.

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

9=12I+16q+2dIdt.

Differentiating with respect to t, the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

ddt(9)=ddt(12I+16q+2dIdt)0=12dIdt+16dqdt+2d2Idt2,

which, when substituting in I=dqdt, gives

d2Idt2+6dIdt+8I=0.

The given equation is a second-order linear homogeneous equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must take a linear combination of two linearly independent solutions.

Assuming the solutions take the form I=eλt, we obtain two solutions, namely, I=e−4t and I=e−2t. So, the general solution in our case is

I(t)=Ae−4t+Be−2t.

We're told that the circuit starts with an initial charge of 14C on the capacitor and an initial current of 1A. Now, solving the Kirchhoff's law equation for dIdt, we have dIdt=92−6I−8q.

So, we can apply the initial conditions I(0)=1 and I′(0)=92−6I(0)−8q(0)=92−6⋅1−8⋅14=−72, and solve for A and B.

  • Substituting I(0)=1 into our general solution gives 1=Ae−4(0)+Be−2(0)1=A+B.

  • Differentiating I, we get I′=−4Ae−4t−2Be−2t Substituting in I′(0)=−72 gives −72=−4Ae−4(0)−2Be−2(0)−72=−4A−2B.

Putting the two equations in A and B together gives the following system:

{1=A+B−72=−4A−2B

Solving this system gives A=34 and B=14. Therefore, the equation for the current (in amperes) in the circuit is

I(t)=34e−4t+14e−2t.

q-345162.name: Question 7
q-345162.problem:
The charge $q(t),$ in coulombs, and current $I(t),$ in amperes, in a series RCL circuit are related by the equation

$$
\frac{dI}{dt}+5I+4q=11.
$$

Find an equation for the current in the circuit, expressing your answer in terms of time $t$ (in seconds) only, and given that the initial charge on the capacitor is $\frac{1}{4}\,\text{C}$ and the initial current is $\frac{3}{2}\,\text{A}.$
q-345162.worked_solution:
The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dI}{dt}+5I+4q) & =\frac{d}{dt}(11) \\ \frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+5\,\frac{dI}{dt}+4\,\frac{dq}{dt} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+5\,\frac{dI}{dt}+4I=0.
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear homogeneous equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must take a linear combination of two linearly independent solutions.

Assuming the solutions take the form $I={e}^{\lambda t},$ we obtain two solutions, namely, $I={e}^{-4t}$ and $I={e}^{-t}.$
So, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)=A{e}^{-4t}+B{e}^{-t}.
$$

We're told that the circuit starts with an initial charge of $\frac{1}{4}\,\text{C}$ on the capacitor and an initial current of $\frac{3}{2}\,\text{A}.$
Now, solving the given relation for $\frac{dI}{dt},$ we have

$$
\frac{dI}{dt}=11-5I-4q.
$$

So, we can apply the initial conditions $I(0)=\frac{3}{2}$ and 

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}^{′}(0) & =11-5I(0)-4q(0) \\  & =11-5\cdot \frac{3}{2}-4\cdot \frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{5}{2},\end{aligned}
$$

and solve for $A$ and $B.$

- Substituting $I(0)=\frac{3}{2}$ into our general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2} & =A{e}^{-4(0)}+B{e}^{-1(0)} \\ \frac{3}{2} & =A+B.\end{aligned}
$$

- Differentiating $I,$ we get

$$
{I}^{′}=-4A{e}^{-4t}-B{e}^{-t}
$$

Substituting in ${I}^{′}(0)=\frac{5}{2}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{2} & =-4A{e}^{-4(0)}-B{e}^{-1(0)} \\ \frac{5}{2} & =-4A-B.\end{aligned}
$$

Putting the two equations in $A$ and $B$ together gives the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2}=A+B \\ \frac{5}{2}=-4A-B\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $A=-\frac{4}{3}$ and $B=\frac{17}{6}.$ Therefore, the equation for the current (in amperes) in the circuit is

$$
I(t)=-\frac{4}{3}{e}^{-4t}+\frac{17}{6}{e}^{-t}.
$$

q-345162.html:
Question 7
?

The charge q(t), in coulombs, and current I(t), in amperes, in a series RCL circuit are related by the equation

dIdt+5I+4q=11.

Find an equation for the current in the circuit, expressing your answer in terms of time t (in seconds) only, and given that the initial charge on the capacitor is 14C and the initial current is 32A.

a
I(t)=43e−4t+52e−t
b
I(t)=43e−4t−176e−t
c
I(t)=−43e−4t+176e−t
d
I(t)=176e−4t+43e−t
e
I(t)=−52e−4t+176e−t
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The current I, measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge q, measured in coulombs. I=dqdt

Differentiating the given relation with respect to t, the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

ddt(dIdt+5I+4q)=ddt(11)d2Idt2+5dIdt+4dqdt=0,

which, when substituting in I=dqdt, gives

d2Idt2+5dIdt+4I=0.

The given equation is a second-order linear homogeneous equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must take a linear combination of two linearly independent solutions.

Assuming the solutions take the form I=eλt, we obtain two solutions, namely, I=e−4t and I=e−t. So, the general solution in our case is

I(t)=Ae−4t+Be−t.

We're told that the circuit starts with an initial charge of 14C on the capacitor and an initial current of 32A. Now, solving the given relation for dIdt, we have dIdt=11−5I−4q.

So, we can apply the initial conditions I(0)=32 and I′(0)=11−5I(0)−4q(0)=11−5⋅32−4⋅14=52, and solve for A and B.

  • Substituting I(0)=32 into our general solution gives 32=Ae−4(0)+Be−1(0)32=A+B.

  • Differentiating I, we get I′=−4Ae−4t−Be−t Substituting in I′(0)=52 gives 52=−4Ae−4(0)−Be−1(0)52=−4A−B.

Putting the two equations in A and B together gives the following system:

{32=A+B52=−4A−B

Solving this system gives A=−43 and B=176. Therefore, the equation for the current (in amperes) in the circuit is

I(t)=−43e−4t+176e−t.

q-344036.name: Question 8
q-344036.problem:
The charge $q(t),$ in coulombs, and current $I(t),$ in amperes, in a series RCL circuit are related by the equation

$$
\frac{dI}{dt}+5I+6q=12.
$$

Find an equation for the current in the circuit, expressing your answer in terms of time $t$ (in seconds) only, and given that the initial charge on the capacitor is $\frac{9}{20}\,\text{C}$ and the initial current is $\frac{9}{10}\,\text{A}.$
q-344036.worked_solution:
The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dI}{dt}+5I+6q) & =\frac{d}{dt}(12) \\ \frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+5\,\frac{dI}{dt}+6\,\frac{dq}{dt} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+5\,\frac{dI}{dt}+6I=0.
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear homogeneous equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must take a linear combination of two linearly independent solutions.

Assuming the solutions take the form $I={e}^{\lambda t},$ we obtain two solutions, namely, $I={e}^{-3t}$ and $I={e}^{-2t}.$
So, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)=A{e}^{-3t}+B{e}^{-2t}.
$$

We're told that the circuit starts with an initial charge of $\frac{9}{20}\,\text{C}$ on the capacitor and an initial current of $\frac{9}{10}\,\text{A}.$
Now, solving the given relation for $\frac{dI}{dt},$ we have

$$
\frac{dI}{dt}=12-5I-6q.
$$

So, we can apply the initial conditions $I(0)=\frac{9}{10}$ and 

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}^{′}(0) & =12-5I(0)-6q(0) \\  & =12-5\cdot \frac{9}{10}-6\cdot \frac{9}{20} \\  & =\frac{24}{5},\end{aligned}
$$

and solve for $A$ and $B.$

- Substituting $I(0)=\frac{9}{10}$ into our general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{10} & =A{e}^{-3(0)}+B{e}^{-2(0)} \\ \frac{9}{10} & =A+B.\end{aligned}
$$

- Differentiating $I,$ we get

$$
{I}^{′}=-3A{e}^{-3t}-2B{e}^{-2t}
$$

Substituting in ${I}^{′}(0)=\frac{24}{5}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{24}{5} & =-3A{e}^{-3(0)}-2B{e}^{-2(0)} \\ \frac{24}{5} & =-3A-2B.\end{aligned}
$$

Putting the two equations in $A$ and $B$ together gives the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{10}=A+B \\ \frac{24}{5}=-3A-2B\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $A=-\frac{33}{5}$ and $B=\frac{15}{2}.$ Therefore, the equation for the current (in amperes) in the circuit is

$$
I(t)=-\frac{33}{5}{e}^{-3t}+\frac{15}{2}{e}^{-2t}.
$$

q-344036.html:
Question 8
?

The charge q(t), in coulombs, and current I(t), in amperes, in a series RCL circuit are related by the equation

dIdt+5I+6q=12.

Find an equation for the current in the circuit, expressing your answer in terms of time t (in seconds) only, and given that the initial charge on the capacitor is 920C and the initial current is 910A.

a
I(t)=335e−3t+245e−2t
b
I(t)=152e−3t−335e−2t
c
I(t)=−335e−3t+152e−2t
d
I(t)=152e−3t+335e−2t
e
I(t)=−245e−3t+335e−2t
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The current I, measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge q, measured in coulombs. I=dqdt

Differentiating the given relation with respect to t, the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

ddt(dIdt+5I+6q)=ddt(12)d2Idt2+5dIdt+6dqdt=0,

which, when substituting in I=dqdt, gives

d2Idt2+5dIdt+6I=0.

The given equation is a second-order linear homogeneous equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must take a linear combination of two linearly independent solutions.

Assuming the solutions take the form I=eλt, we obtain two solutions, namely, I=e−3t and I=e−2t. So, the general solution in our case is

I(t)=Ae−3t+Be−2t.

We're told that the circuit starts with an initial charge of 920C on the capacitor and an initial current of 910A. Now, solving the given relation for dIdt, we have dIdt=12−5I−6q.

So, we can apply the initial conditions I(0)=910 and I′(0)=12−5I(0)−6q(0)=12−5⋅910−6⋅920=245, and solve for A and B.

  • Substituting I(0)=910 into our general solution gives 910=Ae−3(0)+Be−2(0)910=A+B.

  • Differentiating I, we get I′=−3Ae−3t−2Be−2t Substituting in I′(0)=245 gives 245=−3Ae−3(0)−2Be−2(0)245=−3A−2B.

Putting the two equations in A and B together gives the following system:

{910=A+B245=−3A−2B

Solving this system gives A=−335 and B=152. Therefore, the equation for the current (in amperes) in the circuit is

I(t)=−335e−3t+152e−2t.

q-345156.name: Question 9
q-345156.problem:
The charge $q(t),$ in coulombs, and current $I(t),$ in amperes, in a series RCL circuit are related by the equation

$$
\frac{dI}{dt}+6I+5q=\frac{21}{2}.
$$

Find an equation for the current in the circuit, expressing your answer in terms of time $t$ (in seconds) only, and given that the initial charge on the capacitor is $\frac{1}{2}\,\text{C}$ and the initial current is $1\,\text{A}.$
q-345156.worked_solution:
The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dI}{dt}+6I+5q) & =\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{21}{2}) \\ \frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+6\,\frac{dI}{dt}+5\,\frac{dq}{dt} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+6\,\frac{dI}{dt}+5I=0.
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear homogeneous equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must take a linear combination of two linearly independent solutions.

Assuming the solutions take the form $I={e}^{\lambda t},$ we obtain two solutions, namely, $I={e}^{-t}$ and $I={e}^{-5t}.$
So, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)=A{e}^{-t}+B{e}^{-5t}.
$$

We're told that the circuit starts with an initial charge of $\frac{1}{2}\,\text{C}$ on the capacitor and an initial current of $1\,\text{A}.$
Now, solving the given relation for $\frac{dI}{dt},$ we have

$$
\frac{dI}{dt}=\frac{21}{2}-6I-5q.
$$

So, we can apply the initial conditions $I(0)=1$ and 

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}^{′}(0) & =\frac{21}{2}-6I(0)-5q(0) \\  & =\frac{21}{2}-6\cdot 1-5\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{21}{2}-\frac{12}{2}-\frac{5}{2} \\  & =2,\end{aligned}
$$

and solve for $A$ and $B.$

- Substituting $I(0)=1$ into our general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =A{e}^{-(0)}+B{e}^{-5(0)} \\ 1 & =A+B.\end{aligned}
$$

- Differentiating $I,$ we get

$$
{I}^{′}=-A{e}^{-t}-5B{e}^{-5t}
$$

Substituting in ${I}^{′}(0)=2$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =-A{e}^{-(0)}-5B{e}^{-5(0)} \\ 2 & =-A-5B.\end{aligned}
$$

Putting the two equations in $A$ and $B$ together gives the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}1=A+B \\ 2=-A-5B\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $A=\frac{7}{4}$ and $B=-\frac{3}{4}.$ Therefore, the equation for the current (in amperes) in the circuit is

$$
I(t)=\frac{7}{4}{e}^{-t}-\frac{3}{4}{e}^{-5t}.
$$

q-345156.html:
Question 9
?

The charge q(t), in coulombs, and current I(t), in amperes, in a series RCL circuit are related by the equation

dIdt+6I+5q=212.

Find an equation for the current in the circuit, expressing your answer in terms of time t (in seconds) only, and given that the initial charge on the capacitor is 12C and the initial current is 1A.

a
I(t)=−34e−t+74e−5t
b
I(t)=74e−t+34e−5t
c
I(t)=34e−t−74e−5t
d
I(t)=74e−t−34e−5t
e
I(t)=74e−5t−34e−t
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The current I, measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge q, measured in coulombs. I=dqdt

Differentiating the given relation with respect to t, the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

ddt(dIdt+6I+5q)=ddt(212)d2Idt2+6dIdt+5dqdt=0,

which, when substituting in I=dqdt, gives

d2Idt2+6dIdt+5I=0.

The given equation is a second-order linear homogeneous equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must take a linear combination of two linearly independent solutions.

Assuming the solutions take the form I=eλt, we obtain two solutions, namely, I=e−t and I=e−5t. So, the general solution in our case is

I(t)=Ae−t+Be−5t.

We're told that the circuit starts with an initial charge of 12C on the capacitor and an initial current of 1A. Now, solving the given relation for dIdt, we have dIdt=212−6I−5q.

So, we can apply the initial conditions I(0)=1 and I′(0)=212−6I(0)−5q(0)=212−6⋅1−5⋅12=212−122−52=2, and solve for A and B.

  • Substituting I(0)=1 into our general solution gives 1=Ae−(0)+Be−5(0)1=A+B.

  • Differentiating I, we get I′=−Ae−t−5Be−5t Substituting in I′(0)=2 gives 2=−Ae−(0)−5Be−5(0)2=−A−5B.

Putting the two equations in A and B together gives the following system:

{1=A+B2=−A−5B

Solving this system gives A=74 and B=−34. Therefore, the equation for the current (in amperes) in the circuit is

I(t)=74e−t−34e−5t.

q-345164.name: Question 10
q-345164.problem:
The charge $q(t),$ in coulombs, and current $I(t),$ in amperes, in a series RCL circuit are related by the equation

$$
\frac{dI}{dt}+9I+18q=25.
$$

Find an equation for the current in the circuit, expressing your answer in terms of time $t$ (in seconds) only, and given that the initial charge on the capacitor is $\frac{1}{6}\,\text{C}$ and the initial current is $\frac{5}{4}\,\text{A}.$
q-345164.worked_solution:
The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Differentiating the given relation with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dI}{dt}+9I+18q) & =\frac{d}{dt}(25) \\ \frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+9\,\frac{dI}{dt}+18\,\frac{dq}{dt} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+9\,\frac{dI}{dt}+18I=0.
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear homogeneous equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must take a linear combination of two linearly independent solutions.

Assuming the solutions take the form $I={e}^{\lambda t},$ we obtain two solutions, namely, $I={e}^{-6t}$ and $I={e}^{-3t}.$
So, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)=A{e}^{-6t}+B{e}^{-3t}.
$$

We're told that the circuit starts with an initial charge of $\frac{1}{6}\,\text{C}$ on the capacitor and an initial current of $\frac{5}{4}\,\text{A}.$
Now, solving the given relation for $\frac{dI}{dt},$ we have

$$
\frac{dI}{dt}=25-9I-18q.
$$

So, we can apply the initial conditions $I(0)=\frac{5}{4}$ and 

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}^{′}(0) & =25-9I(0)-18q(0) \\  & =25-9\cdot \frac{5}{4}-18\cdot \frac{1}{6} \\  & =\frac{43}{4},\end{aligned}
$$

and solve for $A$ and $B.$

- Substituting $I(0)=\frac{5}{4}$ into our general solution gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{4} & =A{e}^{-6(0)}+B{e}^{-3(0)} \\ \frac{5}{4} & =A+B.\end{aligned}
$$

- Differentiating $I,$ we get

$$
{I}^{′}=-6A{e}^{-6t}-3B{e}^{-3t}
$$

Substituting in ${I}^{′}(0)=\frac{43}{4}$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{43}{4} & =-6A{e}^{-6(0)}-3B{e}^{-3(0)} \\ \frac{43}{4} & =-6A-3B.\end{aligned}
$$

Putting the two equations in $A$ and $B$ together gives the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{4}=A+B \\ \frac{43}{4}=-6A-3B\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $A=-\frac{29}{6}$ and $B=\frac{73}{12}.$ Therefore, the equation for the current (in amperes) in the circuit is

$$
I(t)=-\frac{29}{6}{e}^{-6t}+\frac{73}{12}{e}^{-3t}.
$$

q-345164.html:
Question 10
?

The charge q(t), in coulombs, and current I(t), in amperes, in a series RCL circuit are related by the equation

dIdt+9I+18q=25.

Find an equation for the current in the circuit, expressing your answer in terms of time t (in seconds) only, and given that the initial charge on the capacitor is 16C and the initial current is 54A.

a
I(t)=−296e−6t+7312e−3t
b
I(t)=−434e−6t+7312e−3t
c
I(t)=296e−6t+434e−3t
d
I(t)=7312e−6t+296e−3t
e
I(t)=7312e−6t−296e−3t
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The current I, measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge q, measured in coulombs. I=dqdt

Differentiating the given relation with respect to t, the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

ddt(dIdt+9I+18q)=ddt(25)d2Idt2+9dIdt+18dqdt=0,

which, when substituting in I=dqdt, gives

d2Idt2+9dIdt+18I=0.

The given equation is a second-order linear homogeneous equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must take a linear combination of two linearly independent solutions.

Assuming the solutions take the form I=eλt, we obtain two solutions, namely, I=e−6t and I=e−3t. So, the general solution in our case is

I(t)=Ae−6t+Be−3t.

We're told that the circuit starts with an initial charge of 16C on the capacitor and an initial current of 54A. Now, solving the given relation for dIdt, we have dIdt=25−9I−18q.

So, we can apply the initial conditions I(0)=54 and I′(0)=25−9I(0)−18q(0)=25−9⋅54−18⋅16=434, and solve for A and B.

  • Substituting I(0)=54 into our general solution gives 54=Ae−6(0)+Be−3(0)54=A+B.

  • Differentiating I, we get I′=−6Ae−6t−3Be−3t Substituting in I′(0)=434 gives 434=−6Ae−6(0)−3Be−3(0)434=−6A−3B.

Putting the two equations in A and B together gives the following system:

{54=A+B434=−6A−3B

Solving this system gives A=−296 and B=7312. Therefore, the equation for the current (in amperes) in the circuit is

I(t)=−296e−6t+7312e−3t.

q-345277.name: Question 11
q-345277.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14186466/assets/3c08141f91eea5b2d2006926de5239f91630de139fae970147d8267d46429392.png)

Consider the RCL circuit shown above. Given that the current $I(t)$ in the circuit at time $t$ seconds is given by

$$
I(t)=A{e}^{-2t}+B{e}^{-t}+\frac{P}{13}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\frac{Q}{13}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t),
$$

where $A,$ $B,$ $P,$ and $Q$ are constants, find the value of $P+Q.$

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*
q-345277.worked_solution:
The diagram shows a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $20\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $6\,Ω,$ a capacitor of capacitance $0.25\,\text{F},$ and an inductor of inductance $2\,\text{H}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=6\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=6I.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{0.25}=4q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=2\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=2\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$
20\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)=6I+4q+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(20\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) & =\frac{d}{dt}(6I+4q+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}) \\ 60\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) & =6\,\frac{dI}{dt}+4I+2\,\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+3\cdot \frac{dI}{dt}+2I=30\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t).
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${I}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}{I}_{c}}{d{t}^{2}}+3\cdot \frac{d{I}_{c}}{dt}+2{I}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as a trial solution, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{I}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-2t}+B{e}^{-t},
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants.

- Next, we find a particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $3t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also sinusoidal with argument $3t,$ i.e.,

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute this, as well as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d{I}_{p}}{dt} & =-3\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+3\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t), \\ \frac{{d}^{2}{I}_{p}}{d{t}^{2}} & =-9\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-9\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-9\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-9\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))+3(-3\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+3\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t))\,\,\, \\ +2(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) & =30\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ (-7\alpha +9\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+(-9\alpha -7\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & =30\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-7\alpha +9\beta =30\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)) \\ -9\alpha -7\beta =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-\frac{21}{13}$ and $\beta =\frac{27}{13}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=-\frac{21}{13}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\frac{27}{13}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)={I}_{c}(t)+{I}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-2t}+B{e}^{-t}-\frac{21}{13}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\frac{27}{13}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

Therefore, we have $P=-21$ and $Q=27,$ and

$$
P+Q=-21+27=6.
$$

q-345400.name: Question 12
q-345400.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14186466/assets/28bb1b428a1c187234f0baae580c0fd83eba234c869225f78132f8d110d7a2bc.png)

Find, in amperes, the amplitude of the steady state current for the RCL circuit shown above.

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*
q-345400.worked_solution:
The diagram shows a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $3\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $4\,Ω,$ a capacitor of capacitance $0.5\,\text{F},$ and an inductor of inductance $2\,\text{H}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=4\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=4I.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{0.5}=2q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=2\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=2\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$
3\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)=4I+2q+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)) & =\frac{d}{dt}(4I+2q+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}) \\ -12\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & =4\,\frac{dI}{dt}+2\,\frac{dq}{dt}+2\,\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}+I=-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${I}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}{I}_{c}}{d{t}^{2}}+2\,\frac{d{I}_{c}}{dt}+{I}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as a trial solution, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{I}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-t}+Bt{e}^{-t},
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants.

- Next, we find a particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $4t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also sinusoidal with argument $4t,$ i.e.,

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute this, as well as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d{I}_{p}}{dt} & =-4\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+4\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t), \\ \frac{{d}^{2}{I}_{p}}{d{t}^{2}} & =-16\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-16\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t),\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-16\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-16\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t))+2(-4\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+4\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)) \\ +(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)) & =-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ (-15\alpha +8\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+(-8\alpha -15\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & =-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-15\alpha +8\beta =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)) \\ -8\alpha -15\beta =-6\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t))\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =\frac{48}{289}$ and $\beta =\frac{90}{289}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=\frac{48}{289}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\frac{90}{289}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)={I}_{c}(t)+{I}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-t}+Bt{e}^{-t}+\frac{48}{289}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\frac{90}{289}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity ${I}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-t}+Bt{e}^{-t}$ is the *transient current*, since it goes to zero as $t\to \infty .$

- The function ${I}_{p}(t)=\frac{48}{289}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\frac{90}{289}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$ is the *steady-state current*. It governs the current's long-term behavior.

Therefore, as $t\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
I(t)≈{I}_{p}(t)=\frac{48}{289}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+\frac{90}{289}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).
$$

Finally, the amplitude of the steady-state current, in amperes, is given by

$$
\sqrt{{(\frac{48}{289})}^{2}+{(\frac{90}{289})}^{2}}=\frac{6}{17}.
$$

q-345400.html:
Question 12
?

Find, in amperes, the amplitude of the steady state current for the RCL circuit shown above.

Hint: The voltage drop VC across the capacitor is related to its charge by q=CVC, where C is the capacitance measured in Farads.

a
617
b
28917
c
317
d
1217
e
6289
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The diagram shows a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of 3cos⁡(4t)V, a resistor of resistance 4Ω, a capacitor of capacitance 0.5F, and an inductor of inductance 2H.

The current I, measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge q, measured in coulombs. I=dqdt

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

  • The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality R=4Ω. So, VR=4I.

  • The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by q=CVC. Therefore, VC=qC=q0.5=2q.

  • The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality L=2H. Hence, VL=2dIdt.

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation 3cos⁡(4t)=4I+2q+2dIdt.

Differentiating with respect to t, the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is ddt(3cos⁡(4t))=ddt(4I+2q+2dIdt)−12sin⁡(4t)=4dIdt+2dqdt+2d2Idt2,

which, when substituting in I=dqdt, gives d2Idt2+2dIdt+I=−6sin⁡(4t).

The given equation is a second-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

  • To find the complementary solution Ic, we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by d2Icdt2+2dIcdt+Ic=0. Solving using an integration technique, such as a trial solution, we obtain the complementary solution Ic(t)=Ae−t+Bte−t, where A and B are constants.

  • Next, we find a particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument 4t. So, we assume that the particular solution is also sinusoidal with argument 4t, i.e., Ip(t)=αcos⁡(4t)+βsin⁡(4t). To find the values of α and β, we substitute this, as well as dIpdt=−4αsin⁡(4t)+4βcos⁡(4t),d2Ipdt2=−16αcos⁡(4t)−16βsin⁡(4t), into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side: (−16αcos⁡(4t)−16βsin⁡(4t))+2(−4αsin⁡(4t)+4βcos⁡(4t))+(αcos⁡(4t)+βsin⁡(4t))=−6sin⁡(4t)(−15α+8β)cos⁡(4t)+(−8α−15β)sin⁡(4t)=−6sin⁡(4t) Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations: {−15α+8β=0(equating the coefficients ofcos⁡(4t))−8α−15β=−6(equating the coefficients ofsin⁡(4t)) Solving this system gives α=48289 and β=90289. Therefore, the particular solution is Ip(t)=48289cos⁡(4t)+90289sin⁡(4t).

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is I(t)=Ic(t)+Ip(t)=Ae−t+Bte−t+48289cos⁡(4t)+90289sin⁡(4t).

Note the following:

  • The quantity Ic(t)=Ae−t+Bte−t is the transient current, since it goes to zero as t→∞.

  • The function Ip(t)=48289cos⁡(4t)+90289sin⁡(4t) is the steady-state current. It governs the current's long-term behavior.

Therefore, as t→∞, we have I(t)≈Ip(t)=48289cos⁡(4t)+90289sin⁡(4t).

Finally, the amplitude of the steady-state current, in amperes, is given by (48289)2+(90289)2=617.

q-344172.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14186466/assets/0d8f6711f76fa9e55f11087c99d0e626ebc665e0f44beeefe3f67e9d35159618.png)

Find, in amperes, the amplitude of the steady state current for the RCL circuit shown above.

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*
q-344172.worked_solution:
The diagram shows a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $5\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $10\,Ω,$ a capacitor of capacitance $0.2\,\text{F},$ and an inductor of inductance $5\,\text{H}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=10\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=10I.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{0.2}=5q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=5\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=5\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$
5\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)=10I+5q+5\,\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(5\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)) & =\frac{d}{dt}(10I+5q+5\,\frac{dI}{dt}) \\ -15\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & =10\,\frac{dI}{dt}+5\,\frac{dq}{dt}+5\,\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+2\,\frac{dI}{dt}+I=-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${I}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}{I}_{c}}{d{t}^{2}}+2\,\frac{d{I}_{c}}{dt}+{I}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as a trial solution, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{I}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-t}+Bt{e}^{-t},
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants.

- Next, we find a particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $3t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also sinusoidal with argument $3t,$ i.e.,

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute this, as well as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d{I}_{p}}{dt} & =-3\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+3\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t), \\ \frac{{d}^{2}{I}_{p}}{d{t}^{2}} & =-9\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-9\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t),\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-9\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-9\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))+2(-3\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+3\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)) \\ +(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ (-8\alpha +6\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+(-6\alpha -8\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-8\alpha +6\beta =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)) \\ -6\alpha -8\beta =-3\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =\frac{9}{50}$ and $\beta =\frac{6}{25}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=\frac{9}{50}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\frac{6}{25}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)={I}_{c}(t)+{I}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-t}+Bt{e}^{-t}+\frac{9}{50}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\frac{6}{25}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity ${I}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-t}+Bt{e}^{-t}$ is the *transient current*, since it goes to zero as $t\to \infty .$

- The function ${I}_{p}(t)=\frac{9}{50}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\frac{6}{25}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$ is the *steady-state current*. It governs the current's long-term behavior.

Therefore, as $t\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
I(t)≈{I}_{p}(t)=\frac{9}{50}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\frac{6}{25}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

Finally, the amplitude of the steady-state current, in amperes, is given by

$$
\sqrt{{(\frac{9}{50})}^{2}+{(\frac{6}{25})}^{2}}=\frac{3}{10}.
$$

q-345398.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14186466/assets/4b612821f53f661975a8db889792b44a08aff2e5ba6d6cbc3ccb2992ee048b0b.png)

Find, in amperes, the amplitude of the steady state current for the RCL circuit shown above.

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*
q-345398.worked_solution:
The diagram shows a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $50\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $6\,Ω,$ a capacitor of capacitance $0.125\,\text{F},$ and an inductor of inductance $1\,\text{H}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=6\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=6I.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{0.125}=8q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=1\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$
50\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)=6I+8q+\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(50\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) & =\frac{d}{dt}(6I+8q+\frac{dI}{dt}) \\ 100\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) & =6\,\frac{dI}{dt}+8\,\frac{dq}{dt}+\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+6\,\frac{dI}{dt}+8I=100\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t).
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${I}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}{I}_{c}}{d{t}^{2}}+6\,\frac{d{I}_{c}}{dt}+8{I}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as a trial solution, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{I}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-2t}+B{e}^{-4t},
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants.

- Next, we find a particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $2t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also sinusoidal with argument $2t,$ i.e.,

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute this, as well as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d{I}_{p}}{dt} & =-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t), \\ \frac{{d}^{2}{I}_{p}}{d{t}^{2}} & =-4\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-4\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-4\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)-4\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))+6(-2\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)+2\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)) \\ +8(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)) & =100\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t) \\ (4\alpha +12\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+(-12\alpha +4\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t) & =100\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}4\alpha +12\beta =100\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)) \\ -12\alpha +4\beta =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t))\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =\frac{5}{2}$ and $\beta =\frac{15}{2}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=\frac{5}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{15}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)={I}_{c}(t)+{I}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-2t}+B{e}^{-4t}+\frac{5}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{15}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity ${I}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-2t}+B{e}^{-4t}$ is the *transient current*, since it goes to zero as $t\to \infty .$

- The function ${I}_{p}(t)=\frac{5}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{15}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t)$ is the *steady-state current*. It governs the current's long-term behavior.

Therefore, as $t\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
I(t)≈{I}_{p}(t)=\frac{5}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)+\frac{15}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t).
$$

Finally, the amplitude of the steady-state current, in amperes, is given by

$$
\sqrt{{(\frac{5}{2})}^{2}+{(\frac{15}{2})}^{2}}=\frac{5\sqrt{10}}{2}.
$$

q-345412.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14186466/assets/70072e2a4599c8b1b43ff1782ee270076a384657ab02c7aeec1a3ae87c7674fc.png)

Find, in amperes, the amplitude of the steady state current for the RCL circuit shown above.

*Hint: The voltage drop ${V}_{C}$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C},$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.*
q-345412.worked_solution:
The diagram shows a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $13\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)\,\text{V},$ a resistor of resistance $4\,Ω,$ a capacitor of capacitance $0.25\,\text{F},$ and an inductor of inductance $1\,\text{H}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs.

$$
I=\frac{dq}{dt}
$$

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

- The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=4\,Ω.$ So,

$$
{V}_{R}=4I.
$$

- The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q=C{V}_{C}.$ Therefore,

$$
{V}_{C}=\frac{q}{C}=\frac{q}{0.25}=4q.
$$

- The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L=1\,\text{H}.$ Hence,

$$
{V}_{L}=\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation

$$
13\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)=4I+4q+\frac{dI}{dt}.
$$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dt}(13\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) & =\frac{d}{dt}(4I+4q+\frac{dI}{dt}) \\ 39\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) & =4\,\frac{dI}{dt}+4\,\frac{dq}{dt}+\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

which, when substituting in $I=\frac{dq}{dt},$ gives

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}I}{d{t}^{2}}+4\,\frac{dI}{dt}+4I=39\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t).
$$

The given equation is a second-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

- To find the complementary solution ${I}_{c},$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by

$$
\frac{{d}^{2}{I}_{c}}{d{t}^{2}}+4\,\frac{d{I}_{c}}{dt}+4{I}_{c}=0.
$$

Solving using an integration technique, such as a trial solution, we obtain the complementary solution

$$
{I}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-2t}+Bt{e}^{-2t},
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are constants.

- Next, we find a particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $3t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also sinusoidal with argument $3t,$ i.e.,

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute this, as well as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d{I}_{p}}{dt} & =-3\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+3\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t), \\ \frac{{d}^{2}{I}_{p}}{d{t}^{2}} & =-9\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-9\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t),\end{aligned}
$$

into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}(-9\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-9\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))+4(-3\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)+3\beta \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)) \\ +4(\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\beta \operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)) & =39\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t) \\ (-5\alpha +12\beta )\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+(-12\alpha -5\beta )\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) & =39\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-5\alpha +12\beta =39\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)) \\ -12\alpha -5\beta =0\, & (\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))\end{aligned}
$$

Solving this system gives $\alpha =-\frac{15}{13}$ and $\beta =\frac{36}{13}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is

$$
{I}_{p}(t)=-\frac{15}{13}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\frac{36}{13}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is

$$
I(t)={I}_{c}(t)+{I}_{p}(t)=A{e}^{-2t}+Bt{e}^{-2t}-\frac{15}{13}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\frac{36}{13}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

Note the following:

- The quantity ${I}_{c}(t)=A{e}^{-2t}+Bt{e}^{-2t}$ is the *transient current*, since it goes to zero as $t\to \infty .$

- The function ${I}_{p}(t)=-\frac{15}{13}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\frac{36}{13}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t)$ is the *steady-state current*. It governs the current's long-term behavior.

Therefore, as $t\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
I(t)≈{I}_{p}(t)=-\frac{15}{13}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)+\frac{36}{13}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t).
$$

Finally, the amplitude of the steady-state current, in amperes, is given by

$$
\sqrt{{(-\frac{15}{13})}^{2}+{(\frac{36}{13})}^{2}}=3.
$$

Question 15
?

Find, in amperes, the amplitude of the steady state current for the RCL circuit shown above.

Hint: The voltage drop VC across the capacitor is related to its charge by q=CVC, where C is the capacitance measured in Farads.

a
3
b
3613
c
3
d
1513
e
6
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The diagram shows a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of 13sin⁡(3t)V, a resistor of resistance 4Ω, a capacitor of capacitance 0.25F, and an inductor of inductance 1H.

The current I, measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge q, measured in coulombs. I=dqdt

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

  • The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality R=4Ω. So, VR=4I.

  • The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by q=CVC. Therefore, VC=qC=q0.25=4q.

  • The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality L=1H. Hence, VL=dIdt.

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, these values are related by the equation 13sin⁡(3t)=4I+4q+dIdt.

Differentiating with respect to t, the differential equation governing the current in the circuit is ddt(13sin⁡(3t))=ddt(4I+4q+dIdt)39cos⁡(3t)=4dIdt+4dqdt+d2Idt2,

which, when substituting in I=dqdt, gives d2Idt2+4dIdt+4I=39cos⁡(3t).

The given equation is a second-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

  • To find the complementary solution Ic, we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by d2Icdt2+4dIcdt+4Ic=0. Solving using an integration technique, such as a trial solution, we obtain the complementary solution Ic(t)=Ae−2t+Bte−2t, where A and B are constants.

  • Next, we find a particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument 3t. So, we assume that the particular solution is also sinusoidal with argument 3t, i.e., Ip(t)=αcos⁡(3t)+βsin⁡(3t). To find the values of α and β, we substitute this, as well as dIpdt=−3αsin⁡(3t)+3βcos⁡(3t),d2Ipdt2=−9αcos⁡(3t)−9βsin⁡(3t), into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side: (−9αcos⁡(3t)−9βsin⁡(3t))+4(−3αsin⁡(3t)+3βcos⁡(3t))+4(αcos⁡(3t)+βsin⁡(3t))=39cos⁡(3t)(−5α+12β)cos⁡(3t)+(−12α−5β)sin⁡(3t)=39cos⁡(3t) Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations: {−5α+12β=39(equating the coefficients ofcos⁡(3t))−12α−5β=0(equating the coefficients ofsin⁡(3t)) Solving this system gives α=−1513 and β=3613. Therefore, the particular solution is Ip(t)=−1513cos⁡(3t)+3613sin⁡(3t).

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is I(t)=Ic(t)+Ip(t)=Ae−2t+Bte−2t−1513cos⁡(3t)+3613sin⁡(3t).

Note the following:

  • The quantity Ic(t)=Ae−2t+Bte−2t is the transient current, since it goes to zero as t→∞.

  • The function Ip(t)=−1513cos⁡(3t)+3613sin⁡(3t) is the steady-state current. It governs the current's long-term behavior.

Therefore, as t→∞, we have I(t)≈Ip(t)=−1513cos⁡(3t)+3613sin⁡(3t).

Finally, the amplitude of the steady-state current, in amperes, is given by (−1513)2+(3613)2=3.
